title: Using length as an index
summary: Why an array's length is not a valid index, how the mistake fails at run time, and how to find the last element safely.
objectives: Explain why an array with length `n` has valid indices from `0` through `n - 1`.
Predict what happens when code uses `array[array.length]`.
Trace a loop that uses `<=` and find the index that causes a crash.
Fix an array access or loop by reasoning about the valid indices.

blocks.text: An array's `length` tells you how many values it holds. It is not an index you can use to get a value. For an array of length `3`, the valid indices are `0`, `1` and `2`. This mistake often appears when someone tries to get the last value with `values[values.length]`.

blocks.note: The bad line compiles, but it always fails when it runs: the index is one past the end, whatever the array holds. The good line subtracts `1` because indices start at `0`.

blocks.text: It is easy to mix up a count and a position. A length is a count of boxes. An index is the number on one box, starting at `0`. With three boxes, the count is `3`, but the last box is at index `2`.

blocks.caption: `int[] values = {4, 7, 9};`
blocks.name: values
blocks.note: There are `3` boxes. The last box is `values[2]`. The index `3` points to the gap after the final box, not to a value.

blocks.caption: How length 3 relates to the valid indices
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Length is 3] --> B[Valid indices are 0 1 and 2]
  B --> C[The final box is at index 2]
  A --> D[Index 3 is after the final box]
  D --> E[Accessing index 3 fails at run time]

blocks.title: Keep count and position separate
blocks.text: `length` counts the boxes. An index names a box. The last index is always `length - 1`.

sections.title: Trace it one step at a time

blocks.text: A loop can hide the same mistake. Trace each value of `i` and check whether the condition is true. This loop uses `<=`, so it still runs when `i` equals `values.length`.

blocks.caption: Tracing `for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; i++)` when `values.length` is `3`
columns: What the body tries to do

blocks.text: The fourth pass causes the error. The code compiles, then throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` while it runs. Changing the condition to `i < values.length` makes it stop before the invalid index.
In each example, first identify the array's length. Then list its valid indices. This lets you check the access before running the program.

bad.title: Example 1: length used as the last index
bad.error: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3

good.title: Example 1 fixed: subtract one

blocks.note: The array has length `3`, so its valid indices are `0`, `1` and `2`. The bad program compiles but fails at run time when it tries index `3`. The fixed program uses index `3 - 1`, which is `2`.

bad.title: Example 2: loop includes the length
bad.error: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3

good.title: Example 2 fixed: stop before the length

blocks.note: The bad loop prints the three values, then tries to read `values[3]` and crashes. Both programs compile. The strict condition `i < values.length` stops when `i` reaches `3`, before the loop body can use that invalid index.

blocks.text: The same boundary mistake can appear as a direct access, a loop condition, or a negative index. These examples compile, but an invalid array access fails when it runs.

bad.title: A loop reaches the invalid index

good.title: Visit each array element

blocks.note: When `i` becomes `marks.length`, the bad loop tries to use an index that does not exist. The good loop stops before that value.

bad.title: A negative index is not the end

blocks.note: Java does not use `-1` to mean the final element. For a non-empty array, use `marks.length - 1`.

blocks.question: An array has length `4`. What is its last valid index?
blocks.explanation: The indices start at `0`, so an array of length `4` has indices `0`, `1`, `2` and `3`. The last index is `4 - 1`, or `3`.

blocks.question: What happens when this program reaches its final loop pass?
options: It prints both values and stops normally.
It fails at run time when it tries `a[2]`.
It fails to compile because of `<=`.
It prints the value at index `2`.
blocks.explanation: The array length is `2`, and its valid indices are `0` and `1`. The condition also allows `i` to be `2`, so the program tries an invalid access and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at run time.

blocks.question: Which expression gets the final value from a non-empty array named `items`?
blocks.explanation: The last valid index is one less than the length. So `items[items.length - 1]` accesses the final value.

items: An array of length `n` has valid indices from `0` through `n - 1`.
`array.length` is a count, not a valid index for that array.
For a non-empty array, the last element is `array[array.length - 1]`.
Use `i < array.length` to loop over every array element from index `0`.
An invalid index compiles but throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at run time.
